client: I've been dreading this family reunion coming up next month. Ever since that big fight with my cousin last year, just thinking about seeing them again makes my chest feel tight and my hands shaky. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help, since the tension between us is already so real.
therapist: It sounds like this family reunion is bringing up some very real physical reactions of anxiety for you, especially with how softly and hesitantly you're speaking about it. The tension with your cousin seems to carry a lot of weight—would it help to examine what thoughts come up when you picture seeing them again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: My mind immediately jumps to worst-case scenarios - that they'll bring up the fight again in front of everyone, or give me that cold shoulder look all night. Honestly, part of me feels like avoiding the whole reunion would be easier than facing that awkwardness, even though I know my parents would be disappointed.
therapist: I can hear the distress in your voice as you describe these vivid worries—your tone sounds tense and your thoughts seem to be racing ahead to those painful possibilities. When we anticipate social situations with such certainty about negative outcomes, it might help to ask: what evidence do you have that this reunion *has* to unfold exactly as you're fearing?

client: I guess there isn't concrete evidence it'll be terrible...but last time we saw each other at Christmas, the tension was so thick you could cut it. They made passive-aggressive comments all night. Part of me feels like preparing for the worst is just being realistic, you know?
therapist: Your voice sounds strained as you describe those painful Christmas memories—that mix of resignation and heightened worry is completely understandable given your past experience. vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never really thought about how my expectations might make things worse. But you're right - when I assume they'll be cold to me, I probably come across as defensive or closed off too. Still... it's hard to imagine being open and friendly when I'm so bracing myself for their attitude.
therapist: Your voice sounds both anxious and thoughtful as you make this important connection—I can hear how your defensiveness might feed the cycle while also feeling very understandable. That tension between wanting to protect yourself and wanting things to be different must feel exhausting to hold. Would it help to explore small ways you might experiment with a slightly different approach this time?

client: I guess I could try smiling or saying hello first instead of waiting for them to make the first move...but that makes me nervous. What if they ignore me or say something snide? I'm not sure I can handle that rejection in front of everyone.
therapist: Your voice sounds quite shaky and rushed as you share this—I can hear how vulnerable the idea of reaching out first makes you feel. client: That does make me feel slightly less anxious about it...but I still worry that if they respond badly, I'll spiral and spend the whole evening overanalyzing every interaction. I don't trust myself to stay composed if they're rude to me.
therapist: Your voice has that tense, higher pitch that tells me this fear of spiraling really weighs on you—it makes complete sense that you'd want to protect yourself from that painful overthinking. client: I do have some breathing exercises my friend showed me, but in the moment I always forget to use them. My mind just goes blank when I'm anxious. Maybe if I wrote reminders on my hand or something? Though I worry people would notice and think I'm weird.

client: Maybe I could put a small dot on my wrist where only I can see it, as a reminder to take deep breaths. But I'm still not convinced any technique will help when I'm actually in that situation - when my cousin starts being difficult, all my rational thoughts just disappear.

client: I like the idea of an anchor, but I'm scared that in the actual moment, even looking at the dot will just remind me how upset I am. It's like...when my anxiety spikes, I can't even remember that help exists. Maybe I need something more than just a visual cue?
